title: Dulce de Leche
subtitle: Slow-cooked caramel made from condensed milk
excerpt: A rich, thick caramel made by simmering a sealed tin of condensed milk in a pan of water for 3 hours. This foundational recipe is used throughout Argentine baking and desserts. The result keeps in the fridge for up to 2 weeks and is the filling for alfajores, the topping for ice cream and the spread for toast.
sourceNotes: Dulce de leche is claimed by Argentina and Uruguay as a national invention, with a popular legend attributing its creation to an accidental caramelisation of sweet milk in 1829. Whatever its origin, it is now the defining sweet flavour of Argentine cooking and appears in desserts, pastries, ice cream and countless spreads across Latin America.

recipe.batchNotes: Simmer several tins at once in a large pot. They keep in the fridge for 2 weeks.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make up to 2 weeks ahead. Keep the unopened tin in the fridge once cooked.

glossaryTerms.definition: A thick, golden caramel made by slowly cooking sweetened milk until the sugars caramelise. It is used throughout Latin America as a spread, filling and topping.

content.text: , enough to fill 16 alfajores or generously top 6 portions of ice cream. The active time is about 2 minutes; the rest is hands-off simmering. Plan ahead because the tin needs 1 hour to cool before you open it.

The tin must stay submerged in water throughout cooking. If it is exposed to air, the pressure inside can build dangerously. Check the water level every 30 to 40 minutes and top up with boiling water from the kettle when needed. Never open a hot tin. The colour of the caramel depends on cooking time: 2 hours gives a pale, milky caramel; 3 hours gives the deep, dark golden colour you want.
Remove the label from the tin of condensed milk. Place the tin on its side in a large, deep saucepan. Cover with cold water by at least 5cm.
Bring to the boil over high heat, then reduce to a steady simmer. The water should be gently bubbling throughout.
Simmer for 3 hours, checking every 30 to 40 minutes and topping up with boiling water to keep the tin fully submerged at all times. Do not let the water level drop below the top of the tin.
After 3 hours, remove the pan from the heat and leave the tin to cool in the water for at least 1 hour. Do not open the tin while it is hot.
Once the tin is cool enough to handle, open it to reveal thick, dark golden caramel. Transfer to a jar if not using immediately. Store in the fridge for up to 2 weeks.

attrs.symptom: Caramel is too pale and runny
attrs.fix: Reseal the tin (or transfer to a heatproof bowl covered with foil) and return to simmering water for another 30 to 60 minutes. The longer it cooks, the deeper the colour and thicker the texture.

attrs.symptom: Tin is bulging or making noises during cooking
attrs.cause: The tin was not fully submerged and pressure is building from dry heat
attrs.fix: Remove from heat carefully using tongs. Add more water immediately to cover the tin completely. Never open a hot, pressurised tin.

attrs.symptom: Caramel has a grainy texture when opened
attrs.cause: The water boiled too vigorously and the tin was shaken, causing the milk proteins to set unevenly
attrs.fix: Keep the simmer gentle throughout. Vigorous boiling is not necessary and can cause uneven results. Stir the caramel well once opened; it usually smooths out.

content.text: Dulce de leche is on the breakfast table in Argentina every morning, spread on toast or spooned over yoghurt. It goes into medialunas, fills alfajores and tops helado (ice cream) at every gelateria. In Uruguay it is called dulce de leche as well, and the two countries argue about which version is superior. In Brazil the equivalent is doce de leite, slightly thinner and often grainier. All three are worth making once, just to taste the difference.
